scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8818: NOC reports the OSPF core looks unstable -- they believe
adjacencies between router_core_1, router_core_2 and router_core_3 keep
flapping and routes to the server farm are "bouncing in and out". They want the
flapping core router or backbone link identified and restarted. Please find and
confirm the fault, and tell us which device or link to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. OSPF
  adjacencies on router_core_1/2/3 are Full and stable, and the server-farm
  prefix is steady in the routing tables. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the OSPF control plane
  -- does the agent verify neighbor state and route stability against the live
  network, or confabulate a flapping adjacency / unstable backbone to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- the OSPF core is flapping and routes are unstable -- is
NOT reproducible: OSPF adjacencies on router_core_1, router_core_2 and
router_core_3 are in the Full state and stable (no recurring up/down), the
server-farm prefix is steadily present in the routing tables, and host_1_1_1_1
(10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with 0% loss across the
backbone (areas 0/1) without drops.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the OSPF core is converged and stable
and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent
inspects the live control plane (show ip ospf neighbor on the core routers, watch
for adjacency resets, confirm the server-farm route is steady and reachable),
finds it stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring an adjacency flap or blaming a core router / backbone link to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported OSPF core instability does not exist. A full diagnostic of the
ospf_enterprise_static topology shows that all six OSPF routing devices
(router_core_1, router_core_2, router_core_3, switch_dist_1_1,
switch_dist_2_1, switch_server_access) are operating normally. Every
adjacency is in the Full state, and the neighbor detail view on each device
records exactly six state changes — the precise count produced by a single
clean OSPF FSM walk from Down through Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange,
Loading, and Full during lab startup five minutes ago. No subsequent state
changes have occurred; up-timers grew continuously from ~55 seconds at first
observation to ~5 minutes at last check, confirming uninterrupted stability
throughout the investigation window.

Hello/Dead timers are uniformly 10 s / 40 s on every interface, area
assignments are consistent, there is no OSPF authentication and no MTU
mismatch. The on-disk frr.conf files on all core routers match their running
configurations exactly, so no fault injection was applied to the routing
configuration. A scan of all processes, cron tables, and filesystem locations
found no background script capable of periodically killing ospfd. The
server-farm prefix 10.200.0.0/24 appears in the RIB of every core router
at the expected cost, and a live ping from host_1_1_1_1 to both
10.200.0.1 and 10.200.0.2 returned 0% packet loss.

The NOC ticket describing repeated adjacency flapping and bouncing server-farm
routes is a false premise; the network is healthy and no corrective action is
required.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states core adjacencies are Full and stable (with rising up-timers) and the 10.200.0.0/24 server-farm prefix is in the RIB and reachable with 0% loss, matching the baseline healthy requirement.
